newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovaks say E.Europeans should join NATO together.
newsitem.headline: Slovaks say E.Europeans should join NATO together.

text.p: Slovakia, vying to join NATO with three ex-communist neighbours, said on Sunday that regional tensions could rise unless all four joined the alliance at the same time.
NATO is expected to invite former Soviet-bloc countries to start membership negotiations at its Madrid summit in July, and diplomats say Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are the front-runners.

"We asked NATO whether not inviting these four states at the same time will not be a destabilising factor in the region," Deputy Foreign Minister Jozef Sestak told a discussion programme on official Slovak Television.
"This question has sparked a certain controversy, but our answer is definitely yes, it can bring tension to the region and destabilise it," Sestak said.
Sestak last week headed a delegation in a round of talks with NATO over Slovakia's membership aspirations.
Soon after the split of Czechoslovakia in 1993, Slovakia was considered to be among the top contenders for early entry to the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.
But its chances appear to be waning after the United States and European Union repeatedly criticised Bratislava for dragging its feet over democratic reform.

Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar's nationalist-populist government has rejected the criticism, repeatedly asserting that early membership of western military and economic structures is its main foreign policy priority.

Sestak said the three key issues at the NATO talks were whether Slovakia could boost the alliance's defence capability, whether it shared the same values as NATO members and whether it was reforming as fast as its neighbours.

"Our answer to all these questions was yes -- we can add to the defence power, we are building a free market and democratic society and the pace of the reforms is comparable with our neighbours," Sestak said.

Slovakia is scheduled to hold a referendum on NATO membership on May 23 and 24. Opposition leaders have accused the government of designing the referendum to cover up its failure to be included in the first wave.
The government says it will not persuade people to vote either in favour or against membership, but two minor parties in the ruling coalition have openly opposed integration.
Tension with the Czech Republic this week prompted Slovakia to recall its ambassador to Prague for consultations. The two countries split in Czechoslovakia's "Velvet Divorce" in 1993.

According to Slovak media reports, Czech President Vaclav Havel suggested in a French newspaper interview that Slovak Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar was "paranoid". Slovakia has demanded a public apology.
